worksheet.title: More Than One Fix
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.2 — find a bug, then choose the best fix
worksheet.learning_goal: I can fix a loop bug more than one way and say which fix I would choose.

parts.title: Some bugs have two fixes
text: Bit's loop does TOO MUCH. The code repeats two actions, but Bit only needs to do the action half as many times.

There are two good ways to fix it: change the REPEAT COUNT, or change the BLOCKS INSIDE the loop. Both reach the goal — find both, then pick one to explain. Tip: total actions = repeat × blocks inside.

parts.title: Bit should clap 4 times — but this claps 8
parts.output: Each repeat = 2 claps. 4 repeats × 2 = 8 claps. Goal is 4.

parts.title: Find both fixes
parts.prompt: Bit should clap 6 times, but  repeat 6 { clap, clap }  claps 12 times. Fix A: change the repeat count to ____. Fix B: keep repeat 6 but put ____ clap(s) inside. Show each fix gives 6.

parts.title: Hops
parts.prompt: repeat 10 { hop, hop } makes 20 hops, but Bit should hop 10 times. Write Fix A (the new repeat count) and Fix B (the blocks inside). Which one changes fewer blocks?

parts.title: Write it
parts.prompt: Bit should stomp 8 times. The buggy code is  repeat 8 { stomp, stomp }  = 16 stomps. Write the WHOLE corrected loop two ways — one using Fix A, one using Fix B.

parts.title: Challenge — choose and justify
parts.prompt: Bit should clap 12 times. The buggy code is  repeat 6 { clap, clap, clap }  = 18 claps. Find a fix that changes the repeat count (Fix A) and a fix that changes the blocks inside (Fix B). Pick the one you would use and say WHY in one sentence.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: A bug can have more than one correct fix. A good coder finds them, then chooses the one that is simplest or clearest — and can say why.

teacher_guide.title: More Than One Fix
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 7. More Than One Fix — Teacher Guide

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students find a loop bug that has TWO good fixes — change the repeat number, or change the blocks inside — show both reach the goal, then choose one and say why. Often there is more than one way to fix a bug. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start
parts.text: No computer needed — the worksheet shows the code and what Bit should do. Optional: a Scratch-style app (for the block loops) or a free Python-turtle playground (for the shapes) to run the code — you only press Run.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 30 minutes)
text: 1. Show it (you do). A loop that does double the goal can be fixed by halving the repeat OR by removing one inside block.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — Fix A: repeat 3 with two claps; Fix B: repeat 6 with one clap.
3. Let them work. Students give both fixes (Ex 2), write a whole corrected loop (Ex 3), and choose a fix with a reason (Ex 4).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — Fix A: repeat 3 (3 × 2 = 6). Fix B: one clap inside (6 × 1 = 6).
Exercise 2 — Fix A: repeat 5 (5 × 2 = 10). Fix B: one hop inside (10 × 1 = 10). Fix B changes fewer blocks.

Exercise 3 — Fix A: repeat 4 with two stomps = 8; Fix B: repeat 8 with one stomp = 8. Exercise 4 (challenge) — Fix A: repeat 4 with three claps = 12; Fix B: repeat 6 with two claps = 12. Any reasoned choice is accepted.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: thinking there is only one fix. Show that changing the count OR the inside blocks can both work.
Make it easier: check each fix by multiplying repeats × blocks inside.
Make it harder: ask which fix changes the fewest blocks and why that can be better.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
In plain terms: students write and run step-by-step instructions — including a "repeat" instruction — to make something happen.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, find what is wrong, fix it, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child gives two working fixes, shows both reach the goal, and justifies a choice.
